overview.title: 📖 Overview: Second Jubilees and Inherited Fields
overview.subtitle: Arakhin 26a–26b
overview.hebrewSource: הַלּוֹקֵחַ שָׂדֶה מֵאָבִיו, וּמֵת אָבִיו, וְאַחַר כָּךְ הִקְדִּישָׁהּ — הֲרֵי הִיא כִּשְׂדֵה אֲחוּזָּה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf continues chasing down the true scriptural basis for Rabbi Eliezer's view that an unredeemed field never simply passes to the priests, testing and rejecting one reading before landing on another tied to the word 'anymore.' It then asks a pointed follow-up: if the owner missed his chance to redeem during the first Jubilee cycle but redeems during the second, is he now treated like 'another person'? A new mishna shifts to a different scenario — a son who buys his father's field and later inherits it outright — and asks whether the field's status as 'ancestral' or merely 'purchased' depends on the order of the father's death and the son's consecration. The Gemara traces the resulting dispute to a foundational question about what kind of ownership a lifetime usufruct actually confers.

slides.title: 🧑‍🌾 Finding Rabbi Eliezer's Real Reason
slides.subtitle: A rejected reading, and the case that finally locates his source

nodes.content: ❓ Rabba: Rabbi Eliezer splits Leviticus 27:20 into two separate halakhot, so an unsold field never reaches the priests at all
🗡️ Abaye objects: 'does a sharp knife cut through verses?' — you can't just chop a verse in half to make your point
💡 Real derivation: 'anymore' (עוֹד) addresses a specific case — a field that already went to a priest, whom the priest then consecrated, and the ORIGINAL owner comes to redeem it back
✅ Rava's final formulation: the priests only receive a field 'when it goes out' of the hands of another redeemer — never straight from an owner who held onto it himself

slides.title: 🔁 Redeeming in the Second Jubilee Cycle: Owner or 'Another'?
slides.subtitle: A dilemma with two conflicting versions of Rabbi Eliezer's own ruling

lines.speaker: The dilemma
lines.text: If the owner missed redeeming his field in the first Jubilee cycle, but redeems it himself in the second — is he now treated as 'another person,' so the field goes to the priests at the NEXT Jubilee?

lines.speaker: Version 1
lines.text: A baraita: 'Rabbi Eliezer says: if the owner redeemed it in the second Jubilee cycle, it DOES leave for the priests.' — Yes, he's treated like another.

lines.speaker: Version 2
lines.text: A different version: 'Rabbi Eliezer says: it does NOT leave for the priests.' — No, he keeps his own status as owner.

lines.speaker: Ravina to Rav Ashi
lines.text: But doesn't the mishna itself already say priests never enter until 'another' redeems it — implying the owner, anytime, keeps it?

lines.speaker: Rav Ashi
lines.text: Precisely the novel point: without this baraita I'd have assumed the second-cycle owner counts as 'another.' It teaches me he does NOT — he remains the owner in every cycle.

slides.title: 👨‍👨‍👦 New Mishna: A Field Bought From One's Own Father
slides.subtitle: Does the order of death and consecration change everything?
rows: Father dies first, THEN son consecrates the field
Son consecrates FIRST, father dies afterward
Purchased field — returns to the son (as owner) at the Jubilee, no priests involved
Still an ancestral field — because it was destined to become his by inheritance
'A field that he bought, which is not of his ancestral field' (Lev. 27:22) — excludes only what is already ancestral at consecration
Same verse — but 'not of his ancestral field' excludes anything fit to become ancestral, even in the future

slides.title: 🚫 Purchased Fields vs. Priestly and Levitical Fields
slides.subtitle: Two very different relationships to the Jubilee cycle

boxes.title: A Consecrated Purchased Field
items: NEVER transfers to the priests at the Jubilee
Reason: a person cannot consecrate something that isn't fully his — his rights end at the Jubilee regardless
Instead it simply reverts out of consecration when the purchase-term naturally ends

boxes.title: Priests' and Levites' Own Fields
items: May be consecrated and redeemed at any time — before or after the Jubilee, without the ordinary timing restrictions
Their ancestral land relationship isn't governed by the same sale/return dynamic as an ordinary Israelite's

slides.title: 🍇 The Deeper Dispute: Kinyan Peirot or Kinyan Haguf?
slides.subtitle: Why each side needs Scripture for a different half of the case

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Meir needs a verse only for 'father died first, then consecrated' — implying that before that, owning the right to use the field (kinyan peirot) was NOT yet like owning the field itself (kinyan haguf)

2️⃣ R' Yehuda and R' Shimon need a verse only for 'consecrated first, father died after' — implying that for THEM, kinyan peirot already equals kinyan haguf, so the son's ownership needed no upgrade at his father's death

3️⃣ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak refines this: elsewhere, R' Yehuda and R' Shimon actually treat kinyan peirot as fully equal to kinyan haguf too — they still need the verse, just to teach that the field's ancestral character specifically requires the father's death

summary.principle: Rabbi Eliezer's rule that priests never take a field except from the hand of 'another' redeemer is grounded precisely in the word 'anymore,' and applies consistently across Jubilee cycles; meanwhile, whether a field a son buys from his father counts as 'ancestral' or merely 'purchased' turns on subtle questions of timing and on what kind of ownership a lifetime usufruct actually is.

flowSteps.content: 🧑‍🌾 Abaye rejects Rabba's split-verse reading; the true source is 'anymore,' tied to a field a priest already held and consecrated
🔁 The owner redeeming in a LATER Jubilee cycle is still treated as owner, not 'another' — per Rav Ashi's reading of the mishna

columns.content: 👨‍👨‍👦 A field bought from father: R' Meir looks at consecration-vs-death order; R' Yehuda/R' Shimon call it ancestral either way
🚫 A purchased field never reaches the priests; priests'/Levites' own land bypasses ordinary Jubilee timing entirely

flowSteps.content: 🍇 The Meir vs. Yehuda/Shimon split traces back to whether usufruct ownership (kinyan peirot) equals full ownership (kinyan haguf)
🎓 Key Principle: a field's fate at the Jubilee hinges on exact legal ownership at the moment of consecration — inherited, purchased, or destined to be inherited

quiz.q: Why does Abaye reject Rabba's explanation of Rabbi Eliezer's opinion, that an unsold field never reaches the priests?
o: Because Rabba misquoted the verse
Because Rabba's reading splits a single verse into two unrelated halakhot, which Abaye compares to cutting the verse with 'a sharp knife'
Because Rabbi Eliezer never actually held this opinion
Because Abaye disagreed with the halakhic conclusion, not the derivation
quiz.e: Abaye's objection, 'does a sharp knife cut through the verses,' means one cannot simply divide a single continuous verse into two unrelated legal statements — a more coherent, unified reading of the text is required.

quiz.q: According to Rav Ashi's resolution of the dilemma about redeeming in the second Jubilee cycle, is the original owner considered 'another person' if he redeems the field for the first time only during that second cycle?
o: Yes, in all cases he is treated like another person
No — Rav Ashi teaches that the owner is not considered 'another' in the second cycle either, and a baraita was needed precisely to correct the assumption that he would be
The mishna leaves this completely unresolved
It depends on whether the field was sold in between
quiz.e: Rav Ashi explains that without the clarifying baraita, one might have assumed the owner counts as 'another' in the second cycle; the baraita teaches that he does not — he remains the owner regardless of which cycle he redeems in.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Meir in the new mishna, what is the status of a field a son bought from his father, if the son consecrated it BEFORE his father died?
o: It is treated as an ancestral field, exactly like Rabbi Yehuda and Rabbi Shimon hold
It is treated as a purchased field — it returns to the son at the Jubilee and never goes to the priests
It is not subject to any Jubilee-related rules
The consecration is entirely invalid
quiz.e: Rabbi Meir holds that at the moment of consecration, before his father's death, the field was still legally a 'purchased' field for the son, so it is treated as a purchased field even though his father later dies and it would have become ancestral.

quiz.q: Why can a consecrated PURCHASED field never transfer to the priests at the Jubilee, unlike an ancestral field?
o: Because purchased fields are always redeemed before the Jubilee arrives
Because a person cannot consecrate something that is not fully his; his rights in a purchased field always end at the Jubilee regardless of consecration
Because purchased fields are exempt from all Temple laws
Because priests refuse to accept purchased fields
quiz.e: Since a purchased field's owner only holds it until the Jubilee (when it reverts to the original ancestral owner), he cannot consecrate more than that limited interest — so unlike an ancestral field, it can never end up as a gift to the priests.

quiz.q: What underlying legal question does the Gemara identify as the true basis for the dispute between Rabbi Meir and Rabbi Yehuda/Rabbi Shimon over a field bought from one's father?
o: Whether fields can be consecrated by minors
Whether acquiring the right to use and enjoy an item's produce (kinyan peirot) is equivalent to fully owning the item itself (kinyan haguf)
Whether the Jubilee Year applies outside the land of Israel
Whether fathers can override their sons' vows
quiz.e: The Gemara suggests the dispute hinges on whether kinyan peirot (ownership of usufruct/produce rights) is considered equivalent to kinyan haguf (outright ownership of the item) — this determines exactly when the field's legal status actually changes.
